exchanges.question: What should investors take from the recent management changes (Doug and Troy elevated to co-presidents) and does it imply anything for Dimon's tenure as CEO? Separately, how sustainable is the very high investment banking and markets activity, and how risk-on is the firm?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: the board made two co-presidents to prepare them to do far more; it has not changed the timetable; Marianne chose to retire rather than stay. Barnum: investment banking fees were fine but not super-peak, with some pull forward and large IPOs/ECM deals contributing, though the pipeline is quite robust and the activity may be begetting more; he declined to guide. In markets, the particular equities set of events this quarter is hard to imagine repeating; the market is extremely risk on and JPM is a taker of that, balancing client support with caution.

exchanges.question: How is progress toward the 15% retail deposit market share goal, and how might higher-for-longer rates affect the pace? Separately, where are we in the investment cycle (branches, AI, bankers) and what does it mean for medium-term operating leverage?
exchanges.answer: Barnum: wholesale deposit growth was strong in the first half and outperformed expectations (franchise strength plus lending, including BFI and data center activity); consumer deposits still expected to grow low single digits this year, unchanged, with strong net new checking accounts but yield-seeking flows a possible risk; the 15% is an outcome of executing the strategy, with no change to the aspiration. Dimon: expenses are a complete continuation of what has been done for years, no change expected. Barnum: the firm will always invest and returns speak for themselves; no stated end point to the investment cycle or operating leverage figure.

exchanges.question: What drove the upward revision to NII ex-Markets and what is the cadence in Q3 and Q4 and the exit rate? Why is markets NII guided higher even though rate expectations are higher?
exchanges.answer: NII ex-Markets was revised from $95 billion to $96.5 billion for the full year, implying a higher exit run rate if the forward curve plays out; the biggest driver is deposit balances across wholesale and consumer, plus mix shift toward slightly higher margin, with higher short- and long-end rates a smaller part and consumer betas outperforming the model. Markets NII is liability sensitive and would have fallen on higher rates, but is forecast up due to lower non-interest-bearing financing assets in the second half. Raising CIB equity allocation moves about $150 million of NII from ex-Markets into markets NII, which would not be offset on the bottom line.

exchanges.question: What characteristics are Dimon and the board looking for in the next CEO? Should investors view Dimon's remaining tenure as fixed or rolling, given that Marianne's departure may read as an extension?
exchanges.answer: Dimon said the timing is essentially the same and up to the board; he listed management, people skills, analytics, detail, culture, curiosity, heart, grit, work ethic and the ability to deal with CEOs and prime ministers, noting no one has all of them and he has two exceptional co-presidents, COO Jen Piepszak and Mary Erdoes running AWM. Asked what no change in timing means, he said whatever he said last time stands: several years, plus or minus, up to the board. He did not say whether the date is fixed or rolling.

exchanges.question: Year-to-date adjusted operating leverage is negative; over the intermediate term can expense growth slow and operating leverage become likely given AI and technology? Separately, any update on regulatory proposals, including the G-SIB surcharge and Basel III?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: forever increasing operating leverage is a crazy notion; AI has gives and takes and cannot be projected, but growth might slow in 2027 or 2028; benefits of AI will accrue to customers, not margins. On regulation, Dimon said regulators should do the numbers properly: remove double counts in operational risk and market risk capital (market risk capital is $80 billion or more versus a largest quarterly loss of $1.4 billion), fix G-SIB calibration back to 2015 and short-term wholesale funding. Barnum: the short-term wholesale funding change disproportionately burdens banks like JPM and Bank of America versus former investment bank competitors.

exchanges.question: Is this as good as it gets, or are we earlier in the cycle given AI, defense spending and supply chains? Is there a tipping point where deposit volumes and betas change if rates rise a certain amount?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: it is getting close to as good as it gets, but nobody knows how long it lasts. Barnum: the tipping point is unknown; deposit rate-paid convexity (negative for consumer) has not shown up yet but must kick in at some point; stress tests model an acceleration in rate paid, and one should not be naive about higher rates since a 7% rate environment would not be great if the deposit franchise had to be repurchased. Dimon added the firm assumes some of that.

exchanges.question: Is negative operating leverage the right framing when revenue grew 15% and dollars are positive, given high marginal returns on incremental revenue? Separately, what gives confidence Troy, a trader, can run the consumer business?
exchanges.answer: Dimon agreed operating leverage in dollars was positive and a rapid revenue increase drives big operating leverage. Barnum: expense guidance was raised by $2.5 billion; the first-half capital markets complex outperformed expectations by $6.5 billion with $1.5 billion of additional expense booked, implicitly adding $1 billion for the second half. Dimon said the market is healthy, active and exuberant and he does not know how long it lasts; on Troy, he cited analytics, EQ, culture, and experience in investment banking operations and that big banks run only by investment bankers can suffer. Barnum corrected that Troy was an options trader.

exchanges.question: Are we underestimating AI's efficiency potential, as with Block cutting 40% of its workforce, and could banks operate with a much leaner structure? On equities, what was most exceptional this quarter and hard to sustain?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: AI will be used to do a better job for clients with huge efficiency in parts of the company; almost 1,000 use cases, about 50 really important; some discrete areas cut jobs 30% or 40% with most offered jobs elsewhere; benefits will accrue to customers, not ROE rising to 50%. Barnum: equities drivers were obvious and heavily reported: major IPOs, index rebalancing, complicated dynamics in the Korean equity market and Asia activity; repeating that combination seems statistically improbable though it could happen. Dimon noted volumes are visible daily.

exchanges.question: What are you seeing on the consumer and Main Street side, and is capex broadening beyond AI? Why buy back stock at three times tangible book rather than hold more excess capital, and what about M&A?
exchanges.answer: Barnum: some capex and loan growth does not appear AI related, though AI is proliferating widely; consumer spend is robust across income segments with a tax-refund tailwind, delinquencies lower than expected across FICO scores, little support for a K-shape narrative; consumer credit comes down to the labor market, which has been resilient. Dimon: capex is about $4 trillion a year, AI went from $400 billion last year to $700 billion this year, and a little over a trillion is projected next year. On buybacks, Barnum said they buy back less as the price rises; Dimon said he made a mistake mentioning $20 billion last time, it could be far more or nothing, buybacks are an investment decision, the goal is deploying capital at a 17% return, organic growth first, and they remain open to inorganic opportunities (adjacencies, data) with no specifics; Chase UK is being built.

exchanges.question: What is the status and rollout timing of the smart cash tool, and what did the comment about paying more for money mean? What are the aspirations for European consumer banking?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: smart cash is still a test case affecting a narrow segment of accounts where JPM competes for investment and deposit business; tests are coming and something will be seen this year. In Europe, JPM started Chase UK four or five years ago and has about 2.5 million to 3 million customers in the U.K.; Germany (Berlin) is doing better than expected but not yet profitable; investment products added in the U.K. and likely elsewhere, probably credit card; the aspiration is a pan-European digital bank.

exchanges.question: What are you seeing in competitors' credit underwriting; is it getting crazier? Separately, could regulation enter a period of stability, including Basel III endgame and tailoring, that supports bank valuations?
exchanges.answer: Barnum: crazy is too strong, but JPM passed on some data center deals and sees normal competitive pressure while flexing for important clients and holding the line otherwise. Dimon: only a very mild deterioration across revenue-growth assumptions, expense add-backs, more PIK, weaker covenants and rollover risk, in some players more than others; a credit cycle will come with outliers. On regulation, Barnum said stability is desirable and nonpartisan, and he is not convinced regulation is a major drag on valuations for banks like JPM; Dimon wants regulators to focus on real safety and soundness and said resolution recovery does not work.

exchanges.question: Besides revenue-related expense, are other expense categories such as tech or marketing being pulled forward? How nimble can the CIB capital allocation be, is it at peak, and are there internal limits?
exchanges.answer: Barnum: some of that is going on, with ups and downs including marketing he will not disclose; token (AI model) expense is trivial in the first half, forecast to accelerate meaningfully in the second half but still trivial for the full year and not a driver of the outlook revision. He would not discuss internal limit management: capital allocation responds to client demand plus passive effects (market risk capital rises with volatility, prime RWA with equity appreciation), the firm has a ton of excess capital, and the system is flush with capital but less so with liquidity, calling for liquidity regulation adjustment. Dimon said risk standards have not changed.
